**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 92, verses 4–10:**

God's words, ﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾. This is the answer to the oath. God swore by these things that the deeds of His servants are *shatta*, that is, different in their recompense. *Shatta* is the plural of *shatit*, like *marda* is the plural of *marid*. The differing thing is called *shatta* because some parts of it are far apart from other parts. *Shatat* means distance and separation. It is as if it were said: your deeds are such that some parts are far from others, because some of them are misguidance and some are guidance, some lead to Paradise and some lead to the Fire. So the difference between them is great. Similar to this verse is His words: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal﴾ [al-Hashr 59:20], and His words: ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is defiant? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:18], and His words: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will treat them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-Jathiyah 45:21], and He said: ﴿Nor is the shade and nor is the heat﴾ [Fatir 35:21]. The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Abu Sufyan.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the meaning of the difference in deeds in what we have mentioned, namely the praiseworthy and blameworthy outcome, and the reward and punishment. He said: ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ ﴿and affirms the best reward﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾ ﴿But as for he who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient﴾ ﴿and denies the best reward﴾ ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾.

Regarding His words "gives" there are two possibilities:

The first: that what is meant is spending wealth in all kinds of good, such as freeing slaves, ransoming captives, and strengthening the Muslims against their enemy, as Abu Bakr used to do, whether that is obligatory or voluntary. This general usage is like His words: ﴿and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [al-Qasas 28:54], for what is meant by it is all of that as spending in the way of God, whether obligatory or voluntary. God has praised a people, saying: ﴿and they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ [al-Insan 76:8]. He also said at the end of this surah: ﴿And the most pious will be spared it﴾ ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾ ﴿and for no one has he any favor to be repaid﴾ ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl 92:17–20].

The second: that His words "gives" include giving the rights of wealth and giving the rights of the self in obedience to God, the Exalted. It is said: "So-and-so gave obedience," and "So-and-so gave ease." As for His words "and fears God," it points to avoiding everything that is not appropriate. We have already mentioned whether it is a condition of being pious that one avoid minor sins or not, in the explanation of His words: ﴿a guidance for the pious﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:2].

As for His words "affirms the best reward," the best reward (*al-husna*) has several meanings:

The first: it is the statement "There is no god but God." The meaning is: as for he who gives, fears God, and affirms monotheism and prophethood, the best reward is attained for him. This is because giving wealth and avoiding prohibitions are of no benefit with disbelief. This is like His words: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [al-Balad 90:14] up to His words: ﴿then he became one of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad 90:17].

The second: the best reward is an expression for what God has obligated upon bodies and wealth in acts of worship. It is as if it were said: he gives in the way of God, avoids what is prohibited, and affirms the laws. So it is known that God did not legislate them except for the aspects of goodness and benefit in them.

The third: the best reward is the replacement (*khalaf*) which God promised in His words: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba' 34:39]. The meaning is: he gives from his wealth in obedience to God, affirming what God promised him of a good replacement. This is because He said: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:261]. Since the replacement is greater, the expression "best reward" may be applied to it. According to this meaning, His words "denies the best reward" mean that he did not affirm the replacement, so he was miserly with his wealth due to his bad opinion of the One worshipped. Some have said: "Bad opinion of the One worshipped prevented what was present." It is narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "There is no day on which the sun sets except that two angels call out, which all of God's creatures hear except the two worlds (humans and jinn): 'O God, give every spender a replacement, and every withholder a loss.'"

The fourth: the best reward is the reward itself. It has also been said that it is Paradise, and the meaning is one. Qatadah said: "He affirmed God's promise and acted for that promised thing." Al-Qaffal said: in general, the word *husna* encompasses every good quality. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Do you await for us except one of the two best outcomes?﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:52], meaning victory or martyrdom. He also said: ﴿And whoever earns a good deed, We will increase for him good in it﴾ [al-Shura 42:23], so He named the multiplication of reward *husna*. And He said: ﴿Indeed, for Me with Him is the best reward﴾ [Fussilat 41:50].

* * *

As for His words "We will ease him toward ease," there are several issues:

**The first issue:** regarding the interpretation of this expression, there are several views:

The first: it is Paradise.

The second: it is goodness. And they said that "hardship" means disbelief (*shirk*).

The third: what is meant is that every obligation imposed on him, of actions and abstentions, becomes easy for him, and what is meant by "hardship" is that all of that becomes difficult for him.

The fourth: "ease" is a return to the obedience he performed at first. It is as if He said: "We will ease him to return to giving in the way of God." And they said that "hardship" is its opposite, meaning: We will ease him to return to stinginess and refusal to pay the financial rights. Al-Qaffal said: each of these aspects has a linguistic figurative usage, because actions are judged by their outcomes. So whatever its outcome leads to ease, comfort, and praiseworthy matters, that is from "ease," and that describes all acts of obedience. And whatever its outcome leads to hardship and fatigue, that is from "hardship," and that describes all acts of disobedience.

**The second issue:** regarding the feminine form in the words *yusra* (ease) and *usra* (hardship), there are several views:

The first: if what is meant by *yusra* and *usra* is a collection of actions, the reason for the feminine form is clear. If what is meant is a single action, the feminine refers to the *khallah* (characteristic) or *fi'lah* (act). According to this, whoever takes *yusra* to mean facilitating the return to the obedience a person performed, refers the feminine to *'awdah* (the return). It is as if he said: "We will ease him toward the return which is such-and-such."

The second: the feminine refers to the *tariqah* (path). It is as if he said: "to the easy path and the hard path."

The third: acts of worship are difficult tasks for the body. When the one obligated knows that they lead to Paradise, those difficult acts become easy for him because of his anticipation of Paradise. So God named Paradise *yusra*, and then He gave as the reason for the attainment of ease in performing acts of obedience this *yusra*. His words "We will ease him toward ease" are the opposite of that.

**The third issue:** regarding the meaning of facilitating toward ease and hardship, there are several views. This is because whoever interprets *yusra* as Paradise interprets facilitating toward *yusra* as God's admitting them into Paradise with ease and honor, as God, the Exalted, informed about it in His words: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:23], and His words: ﴿Good you are; so enter it, abiding eternally﴾ [al-Zumar 39:73], and His words: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:24]. As for he who interprets *yusra* as acts of goodness, facilitating them means making them easy for the one who wants them, so that he is not overtaken by the sluggishness that overtakes hypocrites and the hypocritical, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed, it is burdensome except for the humbly submissive﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:45], and He said: ﴿And when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:142], and He said: ﴿What is [wrong] with you, that when it is said to you, "Go forth in the way of God," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:38]. So facilitating was the same as energizing.

**The fourth issue:** the companions (*al-Ashab*, i.e., the Ash'arite theologians) used this verse as evidence for the correctness of their view on *tawfiq* (divine enabling) and *khidhlan* (divine abandonment). They said: God's words ﴿We will ease him toward ease﴾ indicate that He specially favored the believer with this *tawfiq*, which is that He made obedience more preferable for him than disobedience. And His words ﴿We will ease him toward hardship﴾ indicate that He specially abandoned the disbeliever with this *khidhlan*, which is that He made disobedience more preferable for him than obedience. When the verse indicates the occurrence of preference, it necessitates the claim of obligation, because there is no intermediate between doing and not doing. It is known that in a state of equality, preference is impossible, so the state of being less preferred is even more impossible. And when one of the two sides is impossible, the other side must occur, necessarily, since there is no exit from the two sides of a contradiction.

Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, answered the argument from the verse in several ways:

The first: calling one of two opposites by the name of the other is a well-known figurative usage. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura 42:40], and He said: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21]. So when God named the act of the favors that call to obedience "facilitating toward ease," He named the abandonment of these favors "facilitating toward hardship."

The second: it may be understood as attributing the act to the one who causes it, not to the doer. As it was said about idols: ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ [Ibrahim 14:36].

The third: it may be understood as a judgment about it and information about it. The answer to all of these is that it is a departure from the apparent meaning, and that is not permissible, especially since we have shown that the apparent meaning on our side is reinforced by the decisive rational proof. Furthermore, our companions reinforced the apparent meaning of this verse with what is narrated from Ali, peace be upon him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no soul created except that God knows its place in Paradise and in Hell." We said: "Shall we not then rely on that?" He said: "No, act, for each is facilitated toward what he was created for." Al-Qaffal answered this by saying that all people were created to worship God, as He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:56]. Know that this is weak, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, only mentioned this as an answer to their question, meaning: act, for each one is facilitated toward what agrees with God's knowledge. This indicates our view, that what God has decreed for the servant and known about him is impossible to change. And God knows best.

**The fifth issue:** regarding the entry of the particle *sin* (the future marker) in His words ﴿We will ease him﴾, there are several views:

The first: it is by way of gentleness and kindness, and it is from God a certainty and a sure matter, as in His words: ﴿Worship your Lord﴾ up to His words ﴿so that you may become pious﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21].

The second: it may be understood that the obedient person may become disobedient, and the disobedient person may become obedient through repentance. In this case, change is impossible, so the particle is understood differently.

The third: since most of the reward occurs in the Hereafter, and that time has not yet come and no one knows its time except God, it therefore carries a delay. So the particle *sin* was introduced, because it is the particle of delay, to indicate that the promise is deferred and not present. And God knows best.

The differing thing is called *shatta* because some parts of it are far apart from other parts. *Shatat* means distance and separation. It is as if it were said: your deeds are such that some parts are far from others, because some of them are misguidance and some are guidance, some lead to Paradise and some lead to the Fire. The second: that His words "gives" include giving the rights of wealth and giving the rights of the self in obedience to God, the Exalted. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 92, verses 11–12:

As for His saying, ﴿And his wealth will not avail him when he falls to ruin﴾, know that "ma" here may be an interrogative used in the sense of denial (inkar), and it may be a negation. As for ﴿taraddā﴾ (falls to ruin), there are two opinions.

The first: that it is derived from your saying, "taradda min al-jabal" (he fell down from the mountain). God the Exalted said, ﴿And the strangled animal and the one beaten to death﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The meaning, then, is: he falls into the pit when he is buried, or he falls into the depths of Hell. The sense of the verse is: "Indeed, when We ease him toward the difficulty" — which is the Fire — "he falls into Hell. Then what will his wealth, which he withheld and left to his heir, and did not take along with him to his Hereafter, where his poverty and need lie, avail him at all?" As He said, ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 94], and He said, ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone﴾ [Maryam: 80]. He informed that what a person benefits from is what he sends forward of righteous deeds and giving of wealth in its rightful dues, not the wealth he leaves to his heirs.

The second: that "taraddā" is a form of tafa''ala from al-radā, which is destruction, meaning death.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, to Us belongs guidance﴾, know that when He, the Exalted, made them aware that their striving is diverse in its outcomes, and explained what awaits the doer of good in ease and what awaits the wrongdoer in hardship, He informed them that He had fulfilled what was incumbent upon Him of clarification, indication, encouragement, warning, direction and guidance. So He said, ﴿Indeed, to Us belongs guidance﴾, meaning: what is obligatory upon Us in wisdom, when We created creation for worship, is that We make clear to them the ways of worship and explain what makes the worshipper obedient and what makes him disobedient, since We created them only so that We might benefit them, show them mercy, and expose them to lasting bliss. Thus We have done what, in wisdom, was obligatory upon Us.

The Mu'tazilah cited this verse as evidence for their doctrine in several matters:

The first: He, the Exalted, permitted excuses and did not impose upon the one under obligation except what is within his capacity and power. Thus it is established that He does not impose what cannot be borne.

The second: the word "ʿalā" (upon) denotes obligation, so it indicates that something may be obligatory for the servant upon God.

The third: if the servant were not independent in bringing about his acts, the setting forth of proofs would serve no purpose. The responses of our companions to such arguments are well known. Al-Wahidi mentioned another interpretation, transmitted from al-Farra', who said the meaning is: "Indeed, to Us belongs guidance and misguidance," and so the word misguidance was omitted, as in His saying, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], where they protect from both heat and cold. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of 'Ata', who said: "He means: I guide My friends to acting by My obedience, and I prevent My enemies from acting by My obedience," so he mentioned the meaning of misguidance. The Mu'tazilah said: this interpretation is invalid, because of His saying, ﴿And upon God is the direction of the way, and among the ways is that which deviates﴾ [al-Nahl: 9]. He made clear that the direction of the way is upon God, while the deviation of the way is not upon God nor from Him. And know that a full investigation of this has already preceded in that verse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 92, verses 13–16:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ There are two interpretations concerning it.

The first: To Us belongs everything in this world and the Hereafter. Your refusal to be guided by Our guidance does not harm Us, and your being guided does not increase Our dominion. Rather, the benefit and harm of that return to you. Had We willed, We could have prevented you from sins by compulsion, for to Us belong this world and the Hereafter. But We do not prevent you in this manner, because this manner would undermine the obligation (taklif). Rather, We prevent you through clarification, instruction, promise and threat.

The second: To Us belongs the dominion of both abodes; We give whom We will what We will. Thus the happiness of both abodes is sought from Us. The first is more in accord with the view of the Mu'tazila, and the second is more in accord with our view.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes,﴾ ﴿none will burn therein except the most wretched,﴾ ﴿who denied and turned away.﴾

Talazzaa (تلظّى) means: it blazes, flares and glows. It is said: "the fire blazed (talazzat al-nar) with a blazing (talazziyan)," and from this Jahannam is named Laza (لظى). Then He clarified to whom it belongs by His saying: ﴿none will burn therein except the most wretched.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf and those like him who denied Muhammad and the prophets before him. It was also said that al-ashqa (الأشقى) carries the meaning of al-shaqi (الشقي), as one says: "I am not unique in it" (lastu fiha bi-awhad), meaning "not one." So the meaning is: none enters it except the disbeliever who is wretched because he denied the signs of Allah. "Turned away" means: he turned away from obedience to Allah.

Know that the Murji'a hold to this verse to argue that there is no threat except upon the disbelievers. The Qadi (al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: it is not possible to apply this verse to its apparent meaning, and three aspects demonstrate this:

The first: It implies that none enters the Fire ﴿except the most wretched who denied and turned away﴾; so it follows that the disbeliever who did not deny and did not turn away must not enter the Fire.

The second: This is an incitement to sins, for it is equivalent to Allah saying to one who believes in Allah and His Messenger, and neither denies nor turns away: "Whatever sin you commit, it will not harm you." This goes beyond incitement to the point of being like permissiveness, and Allah is exalted above that.

The third: His saying, Exalted is He, after this: ﴿And the most righteous will be spared from it﴾ indicates that this apparent meaning is not intended, because it is known from the state of the sinner that he is not most righteous, since that is an intensification of piety, and one who commits the greatest of major sins is not described as most righteous. So if the first indicates that the sinner does not enter the Fire, this second indicates that the sinner does not avoid the Fire, and every accountable person who does not avoid the Fire must be among its people. Since it is established that interpretation is necessary, we say: there are two aspects:

The first: that by His saying ﴿a Fire that blazes﴾ is meant a specific fire among the fires, because they are levels (darakat), in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa: 145]. The verse then indicates that this specific fire will not be burned by anyone other than this most wretched, and it does not indicate that the sinner and others of this description among the disbelievers do not enter the rest of the fires.

The second: that by His saying ﴿a Fire that blazes﴾ is meant all the fires together, and by His saying ﴿none will burn therein except the most wretched﴾ is meant: this most wretched one is most deserving of it, and this additional degree of deserving is not realized except for this most wretched one. Know that the Qadi's aspects are weak.

As for his first statement: it follows that for other than this disbeliever, one does not enter the Fire. Its answer: every disbeliever must necessarily be one who denies the Prophet in his claim and turns away from considering the evidence of that Prophet's truthfulness; so it is true of him that he is more wretched than the rest of the sinners, and that he "denied and turned away." And if every disbeliever is included in the verse, the Qadi's argument falls away.

As for his second statement: that this is an incitement to sin, it is also weak, because for deterrence from sin it suffices that there is blame in this world and the anger of Allah, meaning that He does not honor him, does not exalt him, and does not give him reward; and perhaps He punishes him in another way. So no proof establishes that the means of punishment is confined to entering the Fire.

**The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb, The Keys to the Unseen) on Surah 92, verses 17–19:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the most pious will be spared it, the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, and for whom there is no favour owed to anyone that must be repaid.﴾ The meaning of *sayujannabuhā* (will be spared it) is: it will be kept far away from it and placed on its side. It is said: *jannabtuhu al-shay'* means I kept the thing far from him and spared him from it. There are two issues in this:

**The first issue:** Our exegetes (*mufassirun*) agree that what is meant is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Know that the Shi'a in their entirety deny this report and say that it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him. Their evidence is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who give zakat while bowing in prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 55]. So His saying, ﴿the most pious, the one who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾, is an allusion to what is in that verse: ﴿those who give zakat while bowing in prayer﴾. When some of them mentioned this in my presence, I said: the rational proof is established that what is meant by this verse is Abu Bakr. Its argument is this: what is meant by this "most pious" is the best of creation. If that is so, then it must be that what is meant is Abu Bakr. These two premises, once they are sound, the intended conclusion is sound. We only said that what is meant by this "most pious" is the best of creation because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you in the sight of Allah is the most pious of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. The "most honourable" is the "best", so this shows that everyone who is most pious must be the best. If it is said: the verse shows that everyone who is most honourable is most pious, but that does not require that everyone who is most pious is most honourable. We say: the attribute of a person being most pious is known and observed, while the attribute of his being the best is neither known nor observed. Informing about what is known through what is not known is the good method, but its reverse is not beneficial. So the structure of the verse is as if a doubt arose as to who is most honourable in the sight of Allah, and it was answered: it is the most pious. And if that is so, the meaning is: the most pious of you is the most honourable of you in the sight of Allah. Thus it is established that the "most pious" mentioned here must be the best of creation in the sight of Allah. We say: it must be that what is meant by it is Abu Bakr, because the Ummah is unanimous that the best of creation after the Messenger of Allah is either Abu Bakr or 'Ali. It is not possible to apply this verse to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Therefore its application to Abu Bakr is determined. We only said that it is not possible to apply it to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib because He said, describing this "most pious" one: ﴿and for whom there is no favour owed to anyone that must be repaid﴾.

As for the report, it is that Bilal was a slave of Abdullah ibn Jud'an. He used to curse the idols, so the polytheists complained to him about his action. These two premises, once they are sound, the intended conclusion is sound. We only said that it is not possible to apply it to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib because He said, describing this "most pious" one: ﴿and for whom there is no favour owed to anyone that must be repaid﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 92, verses 20–21:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except seeking the Countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ ﴿and he will surely be satisfied﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿seeking the Countenance of his Lord﴾ is an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it (munqati', disjunctive), since the thing in question is a favour (ni'mah). That is, no one has a favour with him, ﴿except seeking the Countenance of his Lord﴾, like your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." Al-Farra' mentioned another possibility, which is that the verb "spending" (al-infaq) is implied, so that the sense is: "He spends only seeking the Countenance of his Lord, the Most High," like His saying: ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Countenance of God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:272].

The second issue: Know that He, Exalted is He, has made clear that this one, ﴿the most pious, who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾, does not give it as recompense for a gift or a previous favour, because that would be like repaying a debt, and so it has no bearing on deserving additional reward. Rather, he deserves reward only when he does it because God has commanded him to do it and urged him to it.

The third issue: The anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah) held fast to the word "Countenance", and the heretics (al-mulhidah) held fast to the phrase ﴿his Lord, the Most High﴾, claiming that it implies the existence of another lord. The discussion of all of this has already preceded.

The fourth issue: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani mentioned in the Book of the Imamate, and said: The verse revealed concerning ʿAlī (peace be upon him) is: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God; we desire from you neither recompense nor thanks. Indeed, we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾ [al-Insan 76:9–10].

And the verse revealed concerning Abu Bakr is: ﴿except seeking the Countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ ﴿and he will surely be satisfied﴾ [al-Layl 92:20–21]. So the two verses indicate that each of them did what he did for the sake of God. However, the verse about ʿAlī indicates that he did what he did for the sake of God and out of fear of the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾. As for the verse about Abu Bakr, it indicates that he did what he did purely for the Countenance of God, without any desire for reward or fear of punishment mingling with it. Thus the station of Abu Bakr is higher and more exalted.

The fifth issue: Some people said: "Seeking God" means seeking His essence, and this is impossible, so the intended meaning must be seeking His reward and His honour. Others said: There is no need for this implied meaning. The real question of this issue comes down to whether it is possible for the servant to love the essence of God, or whether what is meant by this love is love of His reward and honour. The discussion of this issue has already preceded in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:165].

The sixth issue: Yahya ibn Wassab read (إلّا ابْتِغاءُ وجْهِ رَبِّهِ) with a nominative ending (raf'), according to the dialect of those who say: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." He cited in both dialects the line:

"A land in which there is no companion, except the wild oxen, and except the camels."

As for His saying ﴿and he will surely be satisfied﴾, the meaning is that He promised Abu Bakr that He would satisfy him in the Hereafter with His reward. It is like His saying to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha 93:5]. In my view there is another possibility, which is that what is meant is that he spent only seeking the good pleasure of God, and God will surely be pleased with him. In my view this is greater than the first, because God's being pleased with His servant is more perfect for the servant than the servant's being pleased with his Lord. In sum, both matters must occur, as He said: ﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr 89:28]. And God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best. May God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
